extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism history; readers interested in American press and nineteenth-century U.S. social history
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and analyzes the defining features, practices, and evaluative dimensions of the American penny press (1830s–1850s) as described in a history/textbook chapter. Useful for understanding what contemporaries and historians treat as the standards and innovations of early mass journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic model: penny price and advertising reliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Penny papers sold for a penny (not six cents) and sought large circulation and the advertising it attracted, rather than relying on subscription fees or party subsidies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter repeatedly contrasts the penny press's market-based income (sales + advertising) with earlier subscription/party-financed models. Examples: Sun, Herald, Public Ledger grew rapidly by this model. Implication: evaluate a paper by how its revenue model shifts incentives toward mass readership and advertisers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution: street hawking and cash sales
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers were hawked in the streets each day by newsboys and sold on a cash (nonsubscriber) basis rather than by annual subscription.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text emphasizes street distribution as central to reach and independence ('nonsubscriber plan'). Evaluate distribution mode (newsboy hawking vs subscription) as a criterion for audience reach and editorial independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising policy: laissez-faire acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: Penny papers adopted a laissez-faire approach to advertising, inserting paid ads (including patent medicines) provided they were not 'indecent or improper' in language and leaving truth/intrusion judgments to readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes explicit Boston Daily Times quote defending patent-medicine ads. Anti-pattern: established six-penny papers refused certain ads on moral grounds. Use this to assess papers' commercial openness vs editorial moral gatekeeping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political independence (claimed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many penny papers claimed formal independence from political parties and described themselves as 'neutral in politics' or otherwise not subservient to partisan sponsors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: James Gordon Bennett's 'nonsubscriber plan' is cited: 'Only the penny press could be a free press…entirely ignorant who are its readers.' Evaluate whether a paper's financial/distribution model supported genuine independence or masked other alliances; note that some penny papers nonetheless pursued vigorous political coverage or had declared principles (e.g., Greeley).

rubrics_metrics.name: Content emphasis: news over editorial, facts over opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: The revolution led to 'the triumph of "news" over the editorial and "facts" over opinion' — newspapers made news the primary product rather than partisan editorializing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historic claim: news became the 'point of rivalry' between papers; editorial pages declined in centrality. Evaluate papers by proportion and prominence of reported news vs editorial content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novel news genres: police, courts, streets, private households
rubrics_metrics.description: For the first time papers regularly printed reports from the police, courts, streets, and private households — expanding 'news' to local and domestic affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: verbatim trial transcripts, police reports, domestic incidents. Use presence of local/city beat reporting and such subject matter as a diagnostic of 'penny-press style' journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paid reporting and beats
rubrics_metrics.description: Penny papers instituted paid reporters and assigned beats (police courts, commercial district, churches, high society, sports), hiring correspondents at home and abroad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text cites papers employing multiple reporters, Washington correspondents, European correspondents, roving state correspondents. Criterion: existence and scope of paid reporting staff and established beats indicates professionalization and commitment to original news gathering.

rubrics_metrics.name: News attributes for comparison: accuracy, completeness, liveliness, timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: News product was judged and compared across papers for 'accuracy, completeness, liveliness, and timeliness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Herald boasted of accuracy and timeliness (e.g., exclusive reports, extras). Use these four attributes as evaluative metrics when comparing contemporary newspapers' news quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and 'extras' (breaking coverage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Penny papers competed on speed — printing 'extras' and boasting of getting news earlier than rivals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Herald's extra announcing British forces in Canton a day earlier. Evaluate frequency and impact of extra editions and promptness of reporting as a criterion of competitive news capability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human-interest and everyday-life focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Penny papers emphasized ordinary life and human-interest stories — the everyday as newsworthy, including exotic aspects of other classes' lives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This shift made 'human interest' central: coverage ranged from criminal reports to high-society events. Evaluate content selection by attention to everyday/social life versus elite political or commercial topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blurring public and private: reporting private habits
rubrics_metrics.description: Penny journalism blurred public and private spheres by reporting private habits and social life (e.g., the Tribune's report on Representative Sawyer's lunch habits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text documents political consequences (ousting reporters from House floor). Use the willingness to report private conduct as an evaluative axis for aggressiveness and scope of newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition based on news gathering and exhibition
rubrics_metrics.description: The success of a journal depended 'wholly and absolutely upon its success in getting, and its skill in exhibiting, the news' — news gathering/exhibition became the chief competitive metric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parton/Jennett analysis; newspapers judged by beats, exclusives, and presentation. Evaluate papers by originality and prominence of their news-gathering methods and display techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial reporting ('money article') as analysis rather than raw facts
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'money article' transformed mere market facts into condensed analysis — 'philosophy of commerce' combined with accuracy, brevity, and spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bennett's innovation: analytical financial reporting attracted business readers. Use depth of commercial analysis and clarity as a quality metric for business journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shift from social/political tied income to market-based income
rubrics_metrics.description: Sources of income that depended on social ties or political fellow-feeling were replaced by market-based income from advertising and sales, rationalizing newspaper economics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess a paper's independence and audience orientation by examining whether revenues derive from partisan/legal patronage or open-market advertising and copy sales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circulation size as indicator of influence and success
rubrics_metrics.description: Large circulation (e.g., Sun 15,000/day within two years; Herald and others) was tied to influence and the ability to attract advertisers and prestige.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text gives circulation figures and comparisons; evaluate impact by circulation scale and readership demographics (e.g., middle-class, business elites).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensationalism critique: printing trials and 'immoral' events
rubrics_metrics.description: Six-penny papers accused the penny press of sensationalism for reporting trials, murders, and other events that older papers deemed improper to publish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: verbatim trial transcripts printed across front pages. Use critics' charges as a lens: assess whether extensive reporting of lurid/local incidents constituted sensationalism or democratized news access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Branding shift reflecting editorial personality and agency
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspaper titles shifted from 'Advertiser'/'Commercial' to names like 'Herald','Tribune','Sun' — signaling active, expressive, and editor-personality-driven journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use naming conventions and presentation tone as indicators of a paper's self-conception (passive commercial bulletin vs active news agency).

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising timeliness: daily resubmission and changing copy
rubrics_metrics.description: Bennett's 1847 policy required ads to be resubmitted daily, encouraging timely and changing ad copy and making advertising more responsive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how a paper structures advertising (flat annual fees vs daily resubmission) to judge its market integration and the informational value of ad columns as contemporaneous city 'reports.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural/political context: ties to democratization and market society
rubrics_metrics.description: The rise of the penny press is linked to the emergence of a 'democratic market society' — expansion of market economy and political democracy shaped the papers' audience, content, and organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical criterion: relate journalistic changes to broader social transformations (urbanization, middle-class formation). Use contextual factors to explain why certain journalistic innovations emerged when and where they did.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial personalization and entrepreneurial innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors became known personally — expressing themselves through industry, enterprise, and innovation in news gathering as well as through editorials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter notes paradox: papers became more personal even as news emphasis rose. Evaluate the degree to which editorial persona shapes paper identity and operations (e.g., Bennett's boastful tone, Greeley's mission).
